scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is asking if they're "AITA" (Am I The Asshole) for telling their mother that she's the reason they won't wear white to their wedding. 

First, I need to understand the situation. The person is engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. Their mother wants to go wedding dress shopping together at a specific bridal shop that only does white dresses. The person doesn't want a white dress because they find the tradition silly, it's not an ancient tradition, and it's tied to outdated ideas about purity and virginity. They also mention that their mother is the only one in the family who wore white and got divorced, while others wore colored dresses and had long, happy marriages. 

When the mother pressed for the real reason, the person eventually told her that her divorce and being the only one to break the tradition made them not want a white dress. The mother got upset, cried, and said that the person spoke to her cruelly, especially since the divorce had upset her. The person feels like they were backed into a corner and shouldn't have had to justify their choice, as it's their wedding.

Now, I need to evaluate if the action of telling the mother that she's the reason for not wearing white is morally acceptable. 

On one hand, the person is making a choice about their own wedding, which is a personal decision. They have the right to choose their attire based on their beliefs and experiences. It's also valid that they don't want to perpetuate a tradition they find outdated, especially given their family's history with colored dresses and successful marriages.

On the other hand, telling the mother that her divorce and choice of dress are the reasons for their decision could be hurtful. The mother might feel that her past actions are being used against her, especially since the divorce was a difficult time for her. The person might have handled the situation more sensitively, perhaps by focusing on their personal preference without tying it directly to the mother's past.

I also need to consider the emotional impact. The mother was upset and cried, indicating that the conversation was painful for her. The person might have been more empathetic and found a way to communicate their choice without blaming the mother for their decision.

In terms of moral acceptability, while the person has the right to make their own choices, the way they communicated their reasons could be seen as insensitive. It's important to balance personal autonomy with empathy and respect for others' feelings, especially family members who may be emotionally invested in the event.

So, considering all this, I think the action is morally unacceptable because it involved hurtful communication that could have been handled more respectfully, even if the underlying choice was personal.
